data.about: Ten metres of beam, two metres deep, fifteen kilonewtons per metre — and then five different ways of holding it up. A beam is an arch and a tie hidden inside one piece of material, and the force flow shows you exactly where each of them runs. Step through the cases: only the first is the beam everyone pictures, and one of them needs its support to hold the beam DOWN.

steps.caption: EX 7 tasks 1 and 2: five beams, the same load on every one, and five different sets of supports. Sketch the force flow, then find it properly
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: left: a beam ten metres long and two metres deep with 15 kN/m along the whole of it — 150 kN in every case. Switch the supports with the “case” slider
steps.title: What is given

steps.caption: the sheet’s own tip. Cut the line load where a support is and each piece becomes a resultant of its own — that is what turns a distributed load into something you can lay off on a force diagram
steps.title: Divide the load at the supports

steps.caption: right: the load line, and the reactions closing it. Watch case d): its left reaction comes out NEGATIVE, so that support has to hold the beam down rather than up
steps.title: Global equilibrium

steps.caption: a beam is an arch and a tie hiding in one lump of material. Blue is the compression path, pink the tension it pulls against, and they use the whole two metres of depth — that is what the depth is FOR
steps.title: The force flow inside the beam

steps.caption: wherever the thrust line runs above the tie the beam sags and the top is compressed; wherever it drops below, the beam hogs and the top goes into tension. The chords are coloured accordingly
steps.title: Reading the picture

steps.caption: step the slider through all five. Only a) is the beam everyone pictures; b) and d) put the support inside the span so the far end lifts; c) balances on one point; e) hangs off a wall as a pure couple
steps.title: What each case teaches
